Miniature Size Chart

Every miniature size chart percentage you need for converting STLs between tabletop scales — from 6mm epic to 32mm heroic, 35mm eye level, and beyond — all on one page. These are the numbers I use myself, based on a 175cm human baseline with eye-level measurement. I print on a Bambu Lab A1 Mini. Your mileage may vary.

Don't know your model's scale? Print the scale reference bar and measure it in your slicer first.

Miniature Sizes at a Glance

Every percentage on one page

1:100 to 1:35

Bridging the gap between 15mm wargaming and large scale model kits.

285.7%

The math

(50.0mm / 17.5mm) × 100 = 285.7%

Based on 175cm human baseline, eye-level measurement (160cm).

Scale baselines

  • Source eye level16.0mm Eye
  • Target eye level45.7mm Eye
  • Scale factor285.7%

This is a big jump from 15mm wargaming into large model-kit territory, and it is usually motivated by wanting a single heroic display piece rather than a battalion.

When you would actually do this

Moving a whole 15mm WWII company wargame force up to 1:35 would be absurd — the models would dominate a tournament table. The realistic reason to reach for this percentage is a centerpiece: one tank or one vignette that you want to paint at a scale with generous surface area. The 15mm source was never meant for this, so expect obvious detail scaling, but the chunky model-kit surfaces take the upscale well.

What I watch for

At 285.7% the build volume becomes the real constraint. A small 1:100 tank can grow into a multi-part build at 1:35, so I plan supports and orientation before slicing. The 15mm source detail — antennas, thin gear — upscales into thicker, more forgiving shape, which is a pleasant surprise.

Is 285.7% correct for 1:100 to 1:35?

Yes. 1:100 maps to a 17.5mm figure and 1:35 to 50mm by eye level, so 50 ÷ 17.5 = 285.7%. This is a 2.86x upscale.

1:100 to 28mm

Those tiny 15mm WWII company wargame infantry scaled up to classic fantasy RPG or WWII platoon wargame height.

160.0%

The math

(28.0mm / 17.5mm) × 100 = 160.0%

Based on 175cm human baseline, eye-level measurement (160cm).

Scale baselines

  • Source eye level16.0mm Eye
  • Target eye level28.0mm Eye
  • Scale factor160.0%

This brings the cheapest big-battle scale up to the everyday tabletop standard. The percentage is modest enough that the models stay recognisable, which keeps the conversion practical.

Why people bridge 15mm to 28mm

I see this most when someone wants a 15mm WWII company wargame tank as a bit of terrain or a display piece on a 28mm board. 160% is small enough that the vehicle reads as a 28mm-scale prop rather than an obviously-upscaled toy. Infantry at this jump get coarse, but vehicles and mechs hold up well.

What to keep in mind

At 160% the detail scales up cleanly, which is the advantage of starting small. The main thing I check is whether the upscaled model matches the proportions of its 28mm neighbours — a 1:100 era vehicle usually does, since the ratios are close enough in practice.

How does 1:100 compare to 28mm?

1:100 is roughly 15mm to the eyes, so scaling to 28mm true scale is a 160% uniform upscale. It lands as a plausible 28mm prop or vehicle.

The realistic use

Honestly, nobody paints a whole battalion at this jump. The practical job is converting one or two iconic vehicles — a particular tank or APC — so they can appear on a 32mm board as wreckage, objectives, or scenery. At 182.9% the hull scales up into a solid, printable shape and the extra size hides layer lines comfortably.

A note on era

32mm is a heroic scale with exaggerated proportions, so a historical 1:100 vehicle can look a touch undersized or too simple next to heroic infantry. I treat these as scenery rather than trying to match them figure-for-figure.

Can I run a whole 1:100 force at 32mm?

Technically yes at 182.9%, but the models read more as scenery than as a matching unit next to heroic-scaled infantry.

1:100 to 35mm

Bumping 15mm WWII company wargame infantry to 35mm sci-fi mass-battle skirmish scale.

A clean double-size jump that lifts 15mm wargaming models up to the 35mm band used by sci-fi and fantasy mass-battle games — useful for turning cheap small-scale vehicles into display props.

Why the double is handy

200% is one of the easiest numbers to type because the muscle memory is simple: anything above 100% doubles the linear size. For a single vehicle or vignette destined to sit on a 35mm board, it is a practical, predictable conversion.

Detail expectations

Starting from 15mm means the upscaled plastic (or resin) reads smooth and slightly simplified, which suits 35mm models well. I check the footprint after scaling, because a small-scale vehicle doubled can still be bigger than expected on the plate.

Why is 1:100 to 35mm a clean 200%?

35mm is exactly double the 17.5mm figure that 1:100 produces, so the jump is a straight 2.0x — 200% uniform scale.

The honest answer

Nothing in 15mm wargaming belongs at 40mm as a playable figure. This jump is for study — understanding how a sculpt reads at display scale — or for turning a small-scale vehicle into a centrepiece. At 228.6% the extra size hides FDM layer lines well, which is the upside.

Supports get complicated

A 2.29x upscale turns fine 15mm details into large, heavier shapes, but it also magnifies internal supports and can make removal a bigger chore. I break large pieces into parts before printing rather than fighting a single tall build.

Is 1:100 to 40mm ever practical for play?

No — it is a display or study conversion. 40mm is far outside the 15mm game's intent.

Plan for a big build

1:35 to 28mm

1:35 model-kit soldiers downscaled for WWII platoon wargame or classic fantasy RPG tabletop play.

56.0%

The math

(28.0mm / 50.0mm) × 100 = 56.0%

Based on 175cm human baseline, eye-level measurement (160cm).

Top of head: 61.3%

Scale baselines

  • Source eye level45.7mm Eye
  • Target eye level28.0mm Eye
  • Scale factor56.0%

Turning a big 1:35 model-kit tank into a 28mm wargaming vehicle is one of the most useful conversions in the hobby — and one of the friendliest, because you only ever shrink.

The classic motor-pool trick

1:35 kits are everywhere and often cheaper than wargaming-branded 1:56 vehicles. Scaling to 56% brings a plastic Tiger or Sherman down to sit properly beside 28mm infantry. I lock XYZ to keep proportions true, then weather the hull to blend the glossy kit plastic with matte infantry.

What to watch

Detail survives shrinking beautifully — this is the direction where FDM excels (you're removing material, not exposing it). Thin parts like gun barrels and stowage can get fragile at 56%, so I reinforce or re-orient fragile elements before they thin out too far.

Is 56% the right shrink for 1:35 to 28mm?

Yes. 28mm of a 175cm baseline maps to 50mm for 1:35 eye level, so 28 ÷ 50 = 56.0%.

Why use 1:35 kits for WWII platoon wargame?

They are cheap and abundant, and at 56% they match 28mm infantry well — which is why players run model kit vehicles despite the nominal 1:56 rules scale.

1:35 to 32mm

Detailed 1:35 miniatures brought down to fit in a modern sci-fi epic wargame army.

64.0%

The math

(32.0mm / 50.0mm) × 100 = 64.0%

Based on 175cm human baseline, eye-level measurement (160cm).

Scale baselines

  • Source eye level45.7mm Eye
  • Target eye level32.0mm Eye
  • Scale factor64.0%

When your army is heroic 32mm rather than true 28mm, the same 1:35 kit trick needs a slightly different number — 64% instead of 56%.

Maths and the heroic difference

Heroic scale is bulkier, so a vehicle shrunk to the same percentage as a true-scale setup will look too small under heroic infantry. Landing on 64% keeps the hull proportionally larger to match the beefy soldiers. I scale a printed hull to sit next to one of my own infantry models before committing to the whole vehicle.

Detail and fragility at 64%

At 64% you keep more of the kit's mass than the 28mm variant, so barrels and stowage stay sturdier. It is a sweet spot that balances size match and printability.

Why 64% rather than 56% for 32mm?

32mm heroic is bulkier than 28mm true scale, so the tank needs to stay proportionally larger — 32 ÷ 50 = 64.0%.

Yes, at 70% the model keeps heft and reads well next to 35mm infantry as a display or objective piece.

The 1:48 for WWII platoon wargame favour

Players favour 1:48 over the official 1:56 because modern plastic infantry have grown bulkier, and the slightly larger 1:48 hull reads better under them. At 76.8% the kit becomes a robust 28mm vehicle. I shrink it, then park a printed infantryman next to it to check the visual match before doing the details.

Fragility reversal

Shrinking to 76.8% thins barrels and stowage. I look for the most delicate elements (barrels, antennas, thin armour plate) and may reinforce or re-orient them so the model survives alongside its 28mm mates.

Why do players prefer 1:48 over 1:56 for WWII platoon wargame?

Modern 28mm plastic infantry are bulkier, so the larger 1:48 hull (76.8% shrink) reads better under them than a true 1:56.

Is 76.8% the right 1:48 to 28mm number?

Yes, based on a 175cm baseline where 1:48 is 33.3mm to the eyes and 28mm true is 28mm — 28 ÷ 33.3 = 76.8%.

Why 114.3% is the number

On a 175cm baseline, a 28mm true-scale figure is 28mm to the eyes and a 32mm heroic is 32mm, so 32 ÷ 28 = 114.3%. It is the single most useful percentage for anyone printing proxies for modern sci-fi epic wargames, modern fantasy wargames, or classic fantasy RPGs.

What actually changes

At 114.3% the figure grows ~14%, which matters most in armies where the two scales meet. I measure the eye line before scaling — a '28mm' sculpt that reads 30mm needs a different treatment. After the uniform upscale, check that the model still fits its base, since a 32mm figure on a 28mm hero base can crowd the footprint.

How these numbers are calculated

By kitsorix, 3D printing hobbyist

I use a 175cm human baseline with eye-level at 160cm. This is what most of the fantasy and sci-fi miniature hobby uses. Historical kits sometimes measure to top of head, which is why the matrix includes both where it matters.

The math is simple division. I print the result on my Bambu Lab A1 Mini before I post it. FDM materials are dimensionally stable within 0.5%, so the percentage you see is the percentage you get. Your mileage will vary.

These values are what works for me and what the community reports back as functional. Your printer, filament, and settings may vary. Always print a test piece.

Full methodology and test data →

Technical guide

Why is miniature scale inconsistent?

Five things I learned after mixing up miniatures from six manufacturers and measuring them with a PARKSIDE digital caliper. The numbers on the box rarely match the model.

In this guide

  1. 1Why does a 28mm miniature measure 30-32mm?
  2. 2Why do 1:48 tanks look better with 28mm infantry?
  3. 3Why do miniature hands keep getting bigger?
  4. 4How much height does a miniature base add?
  5. 5How do I calculate scale conversions for 3D printing?

I have been burned by this enough times that I built a calculator. You buy a box labeled "28mm," paint them up, and they look like teenagers next to your existing squad. One company's 28mm is another's 30mm. The industry ruler is made of rubber.

This is not poor quality control. It is scale creep — a decades-long drift where miniatures slowly put on bulk. I have watched players tear their hair out trying to build a coherent army. The truth is that "scale" in wargaming is less a mathematical constant and more a stylistic suggestion. To build a uniform force, you need to look past the label and understand the math.

1

Why does a 28mm miniature measure 30-32mm?

The discrepancy starts with where the manufacturer places their ruler. Historically, a 175cm human mapped to a 1:60 ratio — the "1 inch = 5 feet" standard. Mathematically that is 30mm. So why call it 28mm?

The answer is the reference point. As Alkony notes, manufacturers rarely tell you where they stop measuring:

"A 28mm miniature means that the size of the miniature will be 28mm from the feet of the mini to the chosen reference point."

— Alkony

In most cases that reference point is eye level, not top of head. It is easier for a sculptor to find the eyes than the crown of a head hidden under a helmet. Add the forehead and headgear, and a "28mm" model is actually 30-32mm in practice.

You are often buying 32mm models that have been grandfathered into a 28mm label for historical reasons.

2

Why do 1:48 tanks look better with 28mm infantry than 1:56?

The WWII platoon wargames state the official vehicle scale is 1:56. On paper this is correct for 28mm. Walk into any tournament and you will see 1:48 model kits dominating the motor pool. This is not an accident.

The publisher has an internal inconsistency. Their metal miniatures are traditional 28mm (closer to 1:52 or 1:56), but their newer plastic sprues are actually 32mm. These plastics are taller and bulkier, so a true 1:56 tank looks like a toy next to them. The volumetric bulk of the infantry makes the vehicle look like the crew would not fit inside.

"I believe they fit with the oversized nature of the publisher's newer plastic infantry better than the actual tanks themselves."

— Reddit, community wargaming forum

There is also a fiscal reality: 1:48 model kits are widely available at hobby shops and often cost half the price of official wargaming-branded 1:56 kits.

For the technical hobbyist, 1:48 is a rare win-win: better visual proportions and lower cost. Use my 1:48 to 32mm conversion and see how it looks on your table.

3

Why do miniature hands keep getting bigger?

"Heroic Scale" is not a lack of anatomical skill. It is a functional design choice. From three feet away — the standard tabletop distance — a realistically proportioned 28mm head is roughly the size of a peppercorn.

"From a tabletop distance, a realistically scaled figure will have unintelligible hands and heads, and if they are scaled up to be readable, the feet look tiny."

— Zandoria Studios

Sculptors exaggerate heads, hands, and weapons to make models readable and easier to paint. This has led to what hobbyists call the "marshmallow man" effect.

You can see this in the new plastic German Veteran and US Airborne kits. They are so puffy that they are incompatible with older true-scale kits. A new-style arm on an old-style body looks like a prosthetic from a different species.

Before you commit to a conversion, cross-reference the source scales in my conversion matrix above.

4

How much height does a miniature base add?

The most overlooked factor is not the model. It is the plastic disc it stands on. Infantry are almost always based on 2mm to 5mm thick plastic. Vehicles in historical games are often left unbased.

This creates a 3-5mm false height. A 32mm soldier on a 4mm base has his eye level at 36mm above the table. Next to a 1:56 Tiger tank resting directly on the mat, he towers over the engine deck.

This gap is why official scales feel wrong. The base raises the infantry's effective scale while the vehicle stays grounded.

3D printing is the equalizer. You no longer have to accept the manufacturer's fixed height. You can scale digitally to compensate for base thickness and ensure infantry and armor share the same visual horizon. My Scale Engine accounts for both eye level and top of head methodologies.

5

How do I calculate scale conversions for 3D printing?

Digital manufacturing shifts power from the factory to the player. Using a 175cm human baseline, I bridge the gap between 28mm (classic fantasy / historical) and 32mm (modern heroic / sci-fi) systems. When mixing STL files from different designers, you need to account for both measurement methodology and material physics.

What I do in practice

28mm true scale to 32mm heroic

I set my slicer to 114.3% for eye level, or <span class="text-white font-mono">116.1%</span> for top of head.

Material compensation

PLA and PETG shrink under 0.5% during cooling. I do not add compensation for FDM because the effect is smaller than normal print variation.

The number I actually use

To match a realistic 28mm soldier to a modern heroic system with material cooling accounted for, I land on 115.8%. Your printer may want something different.

You will find these in the conversion details above.

Scale conversion FAQ

What percentage do I scale 28mm to 32mm?
Type 114.3% into your slicer. That is the number for 28mm to 32mm measured to eye level. If you measure to the top of the head instead, use 116.1%. I have tested this on PLA with no additional shrinkage compensation needed.
How big is a 28mm miniature in real measurements?
A 28mm miniature represents a 175cm human at roughly 1:56 to 1:60 ratio scale. The miniature stands about 30-32mm to the top of the head, with the eye level at 28mm. Add 2-5mm for the base thickness and you have the total height sitting on your table.
What is the difference between 28mm and 32mm scale?
28mm is the classic tabletop standard — measured to eye level on a 175cm human with realistic proportions. 32mm heroic scale uses the same baseline but exaggerates heads, hands, and weapons so details read at arm's length. The height difference is only 14.3%, but the added bulk makes them feel a lot bigger on the table. Full conversion guide
What scale is 1:35 in mm for miniatures?
At 1:35, a 175cm human works out to about 50mm to the eyes. That is significantly bigger than 28mm tabletop miniatures — most 1:35 kits are commercial model-kit military vehicles, not wargaming miniatures. If you want to mix a 1:35 tank with 28mm infantry, scale it down to 62.5% in your slicer.
Does PLA or PETG shrink after printing?
Barely. PLA and PETG can shrink 0.2% to 0.5% as they cool from printing temperature. This is small enough to ignore for miniature scaling. I do not add compensation for FDM because over-extrusion and cooling shrinkage tend to cancel each other out.
Why do 1:48 tanks look better with 28mm infantry than 1:56?
Here is the thing — most modern 28mm plastics from the major wargaming publishers and similar manufacturers actually measure closer to 30-32mm. A true 1:56 tank looks undersized next to them. 1:48 model kits match the heroic proportions better, and they are often cheaper than official wargaming vehicles. I use 1:48 for my WWII platoon wargame motor pool and nobody has complained at tournaments. Use my 1:48 to 28mm guide and see how it looks on your table.
What does "Eye Level" vs "Top of Head" mean in miniature scale?
Eye level means measuring from the foot to the centre of the eye — 160cm on a 175cm human. Top of head means measuring to the crown at 175cm. That 15cm gap creates a 5-10% difference in your scale calculations. Fantasy and sci-fi miniatures usually use eye level because helmets and top-knots vary. Historical kits tend to use top of head. The STL scale converter supports both.
How do I scale STL files for different tabletop games?
Find your source and target scales in the conversion details below, type the percentage into your slicer, and lock the XYZ axes to uniform scaling. Always print a test piece before committing to a full batch. The STL scale calculator on the homepage does this automatically — pick your scales, copy the number, done.
